articles.title: Cleveland Browns: Did Todd Monken tip his hand about the QB rotation?
articles.summary: Everyone assumed that Shedeur Sanders would be QB2 against Jacksonville. But what if the HC has another plan in mind?
articles.body:
Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken walked into a situation no head coach wants to find themselves in.

When training camp opened, Monken looked at the quarterback room, and staring back at him were broken-down veteran Deshaun Watson, rookie Taylen Green, and second-year players Shedeur Sanders and Dillon Gabriel.

Monken's task, which he very much chose to accept when he took the job, was to somehow figure out how to name a starting quarterback for the upcoming season.

That decision was made before the final preseason game when Monken went with the veteran Watson in an attempt to get something out of a quarterback who has not been good since 2020.

With that box checked, the next task was to build out the depth chart to determine who would be Watson's backup and who would be the emergency third quarterback on game days.

Gabriel is out, at least for the first four weeks, after coming down with a back injury after a showcase performance against the Chicago Bears in the final preseason game. This left the obvious choice of naming Sanders as the backup and Green as the emergency quarterback.

Monken has still not officially declared how things are going to play out on Sunday when the Browns face the Jacksonville Jaguars in their Week 1 tilt.

Asked about it on Monday before Cleveland's first practice of the week, Monken remarked that things may not be as they appear :

"Could be (Green as the backup). There could be a package where we have him (in the game). It is possible we could use him."

But the Browns could simply roster all three quarterbacks for the game, which would ensure that Green is there if the situation arises, right?

"I don't think…well, if we could afford it, it'd be nice to have five or six quarterbacks up, but three is a lot."

Three is a lot. As in, having three quarterbacks on the active game-day roster is a luxury the Browns may not be able to afford.

Now this could just all be gamesmanship on Monken's part to keep the Jaguars guessing about what the Browns have in store for them on Sunday. Of course, it is doubtful that the Jaguars are losing any sleep over the prospect of facing any of Cleveland's quarterbacks.

Or it could be the latest example of the Browns telling everyone how they view Sanders, which is that he is nowhere near being a starting quarterback and still needs considerable work before they even consider him a viable backup option.

Unless Monken comes out and clearly states the depth chart this week, late Sunday morning when the inactives are announced for the game, has the potential to be a spicy time in Browns Town.

articles.title: Packers’ MarShawn Lloyd Issues Clear Warning Ahead of Vikings Game
articles.summary: Green Bay Packers running back MarShawn Lloyd understands the lack of respect for him around the NFL, but he isn't here for it. The post Packers’ MarShawn Ll...
articles.body:
The Green Bay Packers are all but certain to begin the season without starting running back Josh Jacobs, which means the oft-injured MarShawn Lloyd, who is currently healthy (knock on wood), will finally get the chance to showcase his skills under the NFL spotlight.

Lloyd spoke to reporters about the opportunity on Monday, September 7, during which he sent a strong warning to those around the league who would underestimate him.

"A lot of players don't know me. They'll watch my college tape, if anything. They won't even know anything about me, won't even worry about me," Lloyd said. "But they will eventually at some point this year."

A third-round pick of Green Bay out of USC in 2024, Lloyd has appeared in just one game and amassed just six carries over the first two years of his career — almost entirely due to health concerns.

Kaleb Johnson May Challenge MarShawn Lloyd for Top Running Back Role in Packers' Offense at Some Point

Lloyd is the presumptive starter in Jacobs' absence as the latter attempts to clear up his off-field legal issues, thereby removing himself from the Commissioner's Exempt List, after which he may face a suspension from the league.

But that does not mean Lloyd will have zero competition as the feature back for as long as Jacobs remains sidelined.

Lloyd is the clear-cut favorite to get the majority of the workload heading into Week 1. However, the Packers executed a trade for Kaleb Johnson , a third-round pick of the Pittsburgh Steelers last season, who should at least challenge Lloyd for touches once he gets up to speed in Green Bay's offense.

Johnson struggled during his rookie campaign, falling out of favor with former Steelers' head coach Mike Tomlin and failing to play his way into the good graces of new coach Mike McCarthy, the offensive-minded play-caller who most recently led the Packers to a Super Bowl back in 2010-11.

But Johnson is just 23 years old and has good size for the position standing at six-feet, one-inch tall and weighing 224 pounds. Running back Chris Brooks is also on the roster and currently in a backup role.

Green Bay Run Game Must Contend With Banged Up Offensive Line to Begin Campaign

One issue Llody, Johnson, Brooks or Jacobs — whoever happens to line up in the offensive backfield on any given play — is going to have to deal with is a below-average O-line that is navigating injuries to a couple of important pieces.

Right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele , formerly known as Zach Tom, is the best player in the unit by a wide margin and dealing with knee problems after an offseason surgery. He missed five games last year with injury issues. Left guard Aaron Banks is also dealing with knee problems and remains a question mark for the season opener against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday.

Speaking with reporters on Monday, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur was non-committal about whether either lineman will play in Week 1.

articles.title: Wildlife and access boost planned for Coventry park
articles.summary: Coventry City Council will use developers' money to make the improvements to Longford Nature Park.
articles.body:
Work is due to start improving access and habitats for wildlife at a nature park in Coventry.

Longford Nature Park is a small reserve which the city council has designated as being of high importance to the city.

The improvements will include a new boardwalk across muddy parts of the park, litter-picking and the creation of shallow wetland habitats.

The work is being funded through Section 106 money, paid by developers to councils for major development projects in the area.

Councillor Patricia Hetherton said the improvements would help protect the biodiversity already at the park and make it easier for people to get closer to nature.

"Green spaces like Longford Park play an important role in supporting our health and wellbeing," she added.

Longford Park, as well as being a nature reserve, also acts as a public path, connecting the Coventry Building Society Arena and the Coventry Canal.

The project will be delivered by the council's urban ranger team, working with volunteers from the Friends of Longfofd Park.

articles.title: Solheim Cup 2026: How Team Europe can regain trophy and why tight contest with Team USA is expected at Bernardus Golf
articles.summary: Team Europe look to regain the Solheim Cup after their 2024 loss to Team USA; Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands hosts this year's edition, where Charley Hull and Nelly Korda are the stars in action; watch live from Friday at 6am on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
Anna Nordqvist's European team look to regain the trophy on home soil at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands, live on Sky Sports , two years on from a 15.5-12.5 loss in Virginia and their first defeat in the biennial contest since 2017.

Whereas the Ryder Cup has typically delivered big winning margins in recent editions, aside from last year's edition at Bethpage Black and a brilliant final-day comeback from Team USA, the Solheim Cup has offered the opposite.

The last three Solheim Cups held in Europe have produced the three closest finishes in its history, with the 2015 and 2019 editions both being won by a single point before the 2023 contest produced the first 14-14 tie.

Each gave their own unique drama and excitement, with Team USA mounting a record singles comeback to win in 2015 before Suzann Pettersen drained THAT putt on the 18th green to help Team Europe to Gleneagles glory four years later.

That's without forgetting the thrilling climax - and Europe retaining - in Spain, where Pettersen's side recovered from being swept in Friday's opening session and came back from the brink in the singles to reach the 14 points required.

Add in the 2011 contest in Dublin, where Europe's winning margin was only two because of an injury withdrawal from Cristie Kerr in the singles, and the last four contests on this side of the Atlantic have had a total winning difference of six points combined.

Given the similarities between this year's line-ups in terms of form, world ranking and past Solheim Cup experience, it's just as hard to predict which team may end up lifting the trophy on Sunday evening.

Team Europe regularly play the 'underdogs' role in the Solheim Cup because of the Rolex Women's World Golf Rankings, given the number of American players higher up the standings, although boast more inside the world's top 10 this time than their rivals.

Charley Hull makes her eighth consecutive Team Europe appearance and world No 7 Lottie Woad features as a rookie in name only, having already won two LPGA Tour titles in just over a year as a professional.

Nordqvist does have five of the world's top 35 at her disposal, as Esther Henseleit climbed after her runner-up finish at the AIG Women's Open and both Maja Stark and Celine Boutier regularly contend on the LPGA Tour.

Team USA do have rankings depth at their disposal, with nine inside the world's top 50 and rookie Lindy Duncan the lowest at world No 66, whereas five European players - including all four captain's picks - head into that weekend below that position.

"I firmly believe it will come down to home advantage," Dame Laura Davies, a 12-time Solheim Cup player, told the Sky Sports Golf podcast .. "It's going to be a very loud week with our girls playing in front of a huge audience.

"On paper, the Americans will probably be favourites because they always are because they all play on the LPGA Tour. I just think that home advantage makes such a difference."

Korda or Hull: Which star will come out on top?

Other than Korda's ridiculous start to the LPGA Tour season, where she won four times and finished no worse than eighth in a 10-tournament stretch, there's been very few - in either team - to reach the winner's circle in 2026.

Lauren Coughlin's Aramco Championship success is the only other win by an American Solheim Cup player on the LPGA Tour, while Boutier and Woad are the only two to have won Stateside from the European side.

Hull was a winner on the Ladies European Tour at the PIF Saudi Ladies International in February, with the Englishwoman now a Solheim Cup stalwart and arriving with the bragging rights of thrashing Korda 6&4 in the Sunday singles two years ago.

She already has 15 match wins to her name in Solheim Cups, the most of any player before turning 30 in history, while only Annika Sorenstam has a better winning points percentage of players to have represented Team Europe as frequently.

Davies called on Hull to "step up and lead" Europe again this week, given her experience, power off the tee and care-free attitude, with Nordqvist expecting the world No 8 to have a big role again in their bid to retain the trophy.

"You've just got to let Charley be Charley," Nordqvist explained to Sky Sports . "It was really nice to see how much she really enjoyed the Solheim Cup last time - she lights up the team room just with her personality. I can't wait to see her tee it up."

Can Nordqvist bring best out of rookies?

Nordqvist was encouraged by her own vice-captains to consider naming herself a captain's pick earlier in the season, given her summer results, although the Swede was quick to quash that idea and name four young selections to complete her roster.

A tied-seventh finish at the Evian Championship briefly ignited those discussions, as did top-30 finishes in her next two events, along with Georgia Hall failing to qualify for the first time since 2015 and Madelene Sagstrom missing out due to childbirth.

The experience of Leona Maguire - the hero of their 2021 win on away soil - needs little introduction, while Julia Lopez Ramirez, Nastasia Nadaud and Mimi Rhodes are all rising stars now getting the chance to test themselves on the biggest stage.

"We got some great power in there and I think we're going to be really strong this year," Nordqvist said. "It's going to be a big change, but also I feel like we have such a good core group of girls that's going to make the other players very comfortable and confident."

Both previous occasions that Europe selected three rookies as captain's picks - in 2011 and 2021 - resulted in wins. Nordqvist would love more than to complete that golfing hat-trick.

articles.title: Epson Tour Championship returns to Players Course at Indian Wells Golf Resort
articles.summary: The Epson Tour Championship will return to Indian Wells, California, for a third straight season.
articles.body:
The Epson Tour Championship will return to Indian Wells, California, for a third straight season. The LPGA's top developmental circuit will hold its season-ending event Sept. 28 to Oct. 4 at Indian Wells Golf Resort.

The Players Course was recently renovated and is joined on the property by the Celebrity course, which was renovated ahead of the 2025 championship.

The City of Indian Wells will continue as presenting sponsor.

The top 15 finishers will earn 2027 tour cards for the LPGA. New in 2026 is an 80-woman field and a no-cut format for the 72-hole tournament. The total purse is $250,000 with $100,000 going to the winner. It's the first time the winner of the Epson Championship will earn a six-figure payday.

"As a premier golf destination, we are excited to once again welcome the Epson Tour Championship to Indian Wells," Dr. Toper Taylor, mayor of Indian Wells, said in a news release. "The Epson Tour brings some of the most talented professional women golfers to our community and provides an incredible opportunity for residents, visitors, and golf fans to experience championship-caliber competition right here in Indian Wells."

"Indian Wells has become the perfect stage for the Epson Tour to crown its season, and we couldn't ask for a better partner in the City of Indian Wells," Jody Brothers, general manager of the Epson Tour, said in a news release. "The newly renovated Players Course gives our athletes a true championship test, and the backdrop of the Coachella Valley creates an unforgettable setting for the final push toward LPGA Tour cards. This is where dreams are realized, and there's no place we'd rather do it."

The Indian Wells Golf Resort's Players Course reopened in December of 2025 after a $13 million John Fought renovation. It's a course that Fought first redesigned in 2007. It dates back to the '80s.

articles.title: LIV Golf: Jon Rahm unaffected by 'turbulence' over tour's future
articles.summary: Jon Rahm says he has become "pretty good at dealing with turbulence" as he remains tight-lipped on his LIV Golf future before this week's Irish Open.
articles.body:
Jon Rahm says he has become "pretty good at dealing with turbulence" as he remained tight-lipped on his LIV Golf future before this week's Irish Open.

LIV's prospects are uncertain following the withdrawal of financial backing from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF).

While the 2026 LIV season ended earlier than planned after the cancellation of the team championship in Detroit, Rahm's Legion XIII team-mate Tyrrell Hatton has said he expects the tour to continue next year.

"Yes and no, it hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis a few weeks ago," Spain's Rahm told BBC Sport when asked if he knows what the future holds.

"And there's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell."

Last month, LIV confirmed it was "scaling back operations" and some employees were laid off at the start of September.

"To be fair for us people that joined LIV, I'm pretty good at dealing with turbulence," two-time major winner Rahm added.

After the Irish Open in Doonbeg, County Clare, Rahm will tee it up at next week's BMW PGA Championship - the DP World Tour's flagship event - at Wentworth.

Earlier this year, the DP World Tour struck a deal with several LIV players - including Rahm and Hatton - which enabled them to compete on LIV without incurring sanction, but the agreement only applies to this year.

While fellow major winners Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed - both in the Irish Open field - opted to leave LIV for a PGA Tour return, Rahm said "we'll see what happens" when asked about a route back.

"I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell," he added.

Rahm, 31, is returning to the Irish Open for the first time since his second title at Lahinch in 2019, having also triumphed at Portstewart in 2017 - his first DP World Tour win.

He won twice during the 2026 LIV season to seal his third successive season-long individual title and finished tied second at the USPGA Championship in May.

Having been greeted by windy and wet conditions on the west coast of Ireland on Monday, Rahm says he is "just trying to get comfortable" before bidding to join his illustrious compatriot Seve Ballesteros on three Irish Open wins.

"It truly doesn't matter [how my game feels right now]," he laughed.

"I think it was the second Irish Open that my game felt terrible leading into it and for the first two days and then somehow ended up winning.

"So it really doesn't matter what it feels like Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Just practise especially in a windy day like today. We're just trying to get comfortable with the surroundings.

"For some of us, get over jet lag quickly and get used to it, but I've been playing good golf all year so I'm hoping I can do it again."

articles.title: Sir Tom Jones says he didn't want to leave ITV's The Voice
articles.summary: The Welsh singer has appeared as an on-off coach on the competition since it premiered in 2012.
articles.body:
Sir Tom Jones has said ITV "fired" him as a judge on The Voice, and he did not want to leave as he "loves the show".

The 86-year-old singer from Treforest in Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012.

Following rumours that he may not return to the panel for the upcoming series, Sir Tom said the broadcaster decided a while ago, but he "was told recently".

He said on social media that he had been offered a reduced role - one he was "not thrilled" about.

ITV has been asked to comment, but the Press Association (PA) reported that a source at the show was "hopeful" the singer would return for its upcoming series.

In a social media post, Sir Tom said: "The reason given is because of a financial difficulty with insurance.

"They now say in the press they wanted to 'refresh' the show, and with a new coaching line-up there wouldn't be a chair for me.

"They are offering a much-reduced role where I would make an appearance but without being actually involved from the start, and I'm not thrilled about that.

"So the only thing I know right now is that there's never a good time to fire an 86-year-old who's still pretty good at his job."

The programme's 2027 series was due to begin production soon.

PA quoted a show insider, saying: "ITV absolutely loves working with Sir Tom. They are in talks with him and are hopeful he will return to the series."

In the most recent series of The Voice UK, Sir Tom featured as a coach alongside McFly stars Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones, as well as US rapper Will.i.am and Destiny's Child singer Kelly Rowland.

Sir Tom has appeared alongside many famous coaches during his tenure on the show, including singers Jessie J, Olly Murs, Kylie Minogue and Rita Ora.

He has also mentored three winners on the programme, Leanne Mitchell in series one, Ruti Olajugbagbe in series seven and Anthonia Edwards in series 11.

Sir Tom, who is known for hits including Green Green Grass of Home and What's New Pussycat?, has enjoyed a successful music career stretching over six decades.

He has achieved three UK number one singles and four chart-topping albums, as well as winning one Grammy, two Brits and an Ivor Novello Award.

Sir Tom was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2006 for his services to music.

articles.title: Junior Solheim Cup: Team Europe produce epic singles comeback before Team USA close out 13-11 win at Bernardus Golf
articles.summary: Team Europe won 8.5 points on the final day but fell to a narrow home defeat against Team USA; Anne van Dam's European team briefly threatened the biggest comeback in the event's history; watch the Solheim Cup live on Friday from 6am on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
Morgan Pressel's side had dominated the opening day to take a seven-point lead into Tuesday's singles at Bernardus Golf, leaving them requiring only 2.5 points to retain the trophy and three for outright victory.

The target required was the same Team Europe experienced during last year's Ryder Cup before they clung on to victory, although the visitors were left sweating as Anne van Dam's European side threatened a record-breaking comeback.

Team Europe won 8.5 of the 12 points on offer on Sunday, including England's Annabel Peaford winning three of her last four holes to claim a 1up win over world No 1 Asterisk Talley in the opening match, but fell to their second successive loss.

"It's easy to coach a team this insanely talented," Pressel said. "They are also so clutch in the biggest moments. It was so fun to watch both sides and they all showed so much heart."

How Team USA edged Junior Solheim thriller

Any hopes of a home comeback appeared unlikely when Eliana Saga claimed a 4&3 win over Adriana Garcia Terol and Madeleine Conser beat Lana Guyot 5&4, taking them within 0.5 points of retaining.

Talley had already looked set to earn Team USA's first point of the day when she was 2up with four to go, only for Peaford to par the 15th and birdie the 16th before winning the next two holes and snatch a remarkable victory.

Lauren Crump saw off Amber Lee 3&2 and Anna Ludvova won three consecutive holes around the turn in a 2&1 win over Grace Carter, with Lena Geier claiming a final-hole win over Aubrey Hilgers to earn Europe further points.

Sofia Maier-Borst and Axelle Guillemard beat Amelie Zalsman and Honorine Ferry respectively to keep hopes of an unlikely European victory alive, before Kelly Zhang claimed the winning point for Team USA with a 2up victory over Carolina Perez-Tasso.

Carlota Lopez Minguela closed out a 3&2 success over Iris Lee and Marta Munoz found a penultimate-hole birdie to tie with Anna Fang, while Team Europe reduced the winning margin further after Alice Kong snatched a final-hole win over Lily Peng.

"I'm so proud and I could not have asked them for any more today," Van Dam said. "It's tough. The US team are incredible, but the girls know they gave their all and that's why they are still smiling tonight."

Sky Sports Golf will have at least 12 hours of live coverage from the first two days of the Solheim Cup, with coverage getting under way at 6am on Friday and Saturday ahead of the opening foursomes match teeing off at 6.40am (7.40am local time).

The afternoon fourballs are scheduled to start at 12.05pm (1.05pm local time) on both days, with coverage continuing until after the final putt is holed, while Sunday singles coverage begins at 9am ahead of the opening tee shot at 10.10am.

Sky Sports+ will have live coverage of the closing ceremony from 5.30pm on Sunday, following the Solheim Cup winner being crowned, while the opening ceremony on Thursday at 4.30pm will see the opening-day pairings revealed.

articles.title: Jon Rahm dibuja su otoño y regatea las incógnitas sobre su futuro en LIV
articles.standfirst: El de Barrika quiere jugar los playoffs de Abu Dhabi y Dubai y mantiene la duda con España
articles.summary: El de Barrika quiere jugar los playoffs de Abu Dhabi y Dubai y mantiene la duda con España
articles.body: Jon Rahm afronta el tramo final de 2026 con un calendario cada vez más definido, aunque con una prioridad que está por encima de cualquier torneo. El español, que regresa esta semana al DP World Tour en el Amgen Irish Open, ha confirmado su intención de disputar los dos playoffs de Emiratos Árabes Unidos y mantiene su deseo de jugar el Open de España, cuya presencia dependerá del nacimiento de su cuarto hijo. Un otoño en el que volverá a competir en Europa tras finalizar la temporada de LIV Golf y mientras sigue sin despejarse su futuro profesional. "Lo que quiero hacer no ha cambiado. Juego aquí, juego la semana que viene y tengo previsto jugar Abu Dhabi y Dubai, dependiendo de si se disputan y de lo que ocurra en esa parte del mundo", explicó este martes en Doonbeg, escenario del torneo irlandés. El plan incluye, por tanto, el Irish Open y el BMW PGA Championship de Wentworth, además del Abu Dhabi HSBC Championship, previsto del 5 al 8 de noviembre en Yas Links, y el DP World Tour Championship, del 12 al 15 en Jumeirah Golf Estates. La celebración de las dos citas de Emiratos queda condicionada por la situación bélica en Oriente Próximo. Abu Dhabi supondría, además, una novedad en la trayectoria de Rahm, que nunca ha disputado ese torneo. Su intención de participar en los playoffs tiene también una evidente dimensión deportiva. Son dos citas de gran valor para la clasificación de la Ryder Cup y para la Race to Dubai, que concede diez tarjetas del PGA Tour para la siguiente temporada. Rahm, teóricamente, no necesitaría esa vía para disponer de categoría en el circuito estadounidense, gracias a su victoria en el Masters de 2023, pero terminar entre los 10 elegibles podría convertirse en un argumento adicional de cara a un eventual regreso en 2027. Por ahora, no obstante, se trata de una posibilidad y no de una decisión anunciada por el jugador. La mayor incertidumbre de su calendario se encuentra antes de los playoffs. El Alfred Dunhill Links Championship y el Open de España coinciden con las fechas previstas para el nacimiento de su cuarto hijo, por lo que Rahm no puede garantizar todavía su participación. Aunque inicialmente contemplaba jugar el Dunhill, en su comparecencia de este martes no lo incluyó entre los torneos que confirmó expresamente. "El Open de España dependerá de cuándo decida llegar el bebé. Espero poder estar, pero ya veremos. Es una de esas situaciones en las que la familia siempre está por delante y, por mucho que me guste el Open de España, si tengo que elegir, evidentemente la decisión es fácil. Todo dependerá de cuándo decida llegar el bebé", señaló. El golfista de Barrika ha pasado las últimas semanas centrado en su familia, una circunstancia que también ha condicionado su preparación para el regreso a la competición: "Básicamente he estado ejerciendo de padre. Tengo a mi mujer en casa muy embarazada y está notando mucho este embarazo. Desgraciadamente, no se encontraba demasiado bien, así que por suerte yo estaba en casa y pude ocuparme de los niños". Rahm reconoce que ha tenido poco tiempo para entrenar, aunque considera que ese descanso ha sido positivo después de una temporada intensa: "No me ha dejado mucho espacio para el golf, pero a estas alturas del año, tener un poco de descanso y ocuparse de la realidad y de la vida de verdad es algo muy agradable y necesario. Estaba muy contento de poder estar en casa y cuidar de mis hijo". La comparecencia también dejó una pregunta sobre su situación profesional y la posibilidad de un cambio de circuito. Rahm se remitió a lo que ya había explicado en Indianápolis, última prueba de la temporada de LIV Golf, y no ofreció novedades sobre su futuro. El español continúa vinculado contractualmente a la liga saudí, por lo que su calendario europeo no supone, por sí solo, un anuncio de regreso al PGA Tour. Mientras tanto, el objetivo inmediato es recuperar el ritmo competitivo en un escenario que le trae excelentes recuerdos. Rahm cumple este año diez temporadas como profesional, una década en la que ha conquistado dos grandes, diez títulos del DP World Tour y ha alcanzado el Número Uno del mundo. "He conseguido mucho y estoy muy contento con lo que he hecho hasta ahora. Evidentemente, como competidor, siempre hay momentos en los que pienso que debería haber hecho más. Todos queremos ganar más, pero he tenido mucha suerte de poder jugar a este deporte a un nivel muy alto y espero poder seguir haciéndolo durante la próxima década", reflexionó. El español cree que su evolución ha sido más una cuestión de experiencia y eficiencia que de cambios radicales: "Soy un poco mejor en todos los aspectos del juego, tengo más experiencia y más conocimientos. No diría que puedo pegar golpes que antes no podía, pero sí que soy un poco más eficiente al ejecutarlos. A este nivel, una mejora de medio punto porcentual en cada aspecto del juego puede tener un impacto enorme". Rahm vuelve al Irish Open siete años después de su última participación, con un balance difícil de mejorar: dos victorias y un cuarto puesto en tres apariciones. Ganó en Portstewart en 2017, fue cuarto en Ballyliffin en 2018 y volvió a levantar el trofeo en Lahinch en 2019. Ahora buscará un tercer título que le permitiría igualar a Seve Ballesteros, Bernhard Langer, Nick Faldo y Colin Montgomerie. "No sé qué tienen los irlandeses, pero cada vez que vengo me hacen sentir como en casa", aseguró. "Cuando vienes como golfista profesional y te sientes tan apreciado, es algo único. Irlanda siempre tendrá un lugar muy especial en mi corazón", desveló el español. Su preparación sobre el recorrido de Doonbeg ha sido limitada. El lunes apenas pudo completar tres hoyos por culpa de la lluvia, que le obligó a abandonar el campo en dos ocasiones. Rahm, acostumbrado a competir en links, no parece especialmente preocupado: "Llevo mucho tiempo jugando en links y sé lo que me espera. El viento y la lluvia son lo normal". También mira de reojo a la Ryder Cup de 2027, que se celebrará en Adare Manor, aunque considera que todavía queda demasiado tiempo para convertirla en una preocupación inmediata: "Espero estar representando a Europa en Adare Manor. Me encantaría estar allí, pero queda tanto tiempo que todavía no he pensado demasiado en ello". De momento, su atención está puesta en el jueves, en volver a competir y en comenzar un otoño que puede tener importantes consecuencias para su carrera. El calendario está trazado; el nacimiento de su cuarto hijo y la evolución de su futuro profesional terminarán de marcar el camino.

articles.title: Rory McIlroy: Defending champion expecting 'different' Irish Open with President Trump visit
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy admits this year's Irish Open will feel like a "different" spectacle given US President Donald Trump's anticipated visit during the tournament.
articles.body:
Rory McIlroy admits this year's Irish Open will feel like a "different" spectacle given US President Donald Trump's anticipated visit during the tournament's latter stages.

Trump is expected to attend the event - which is being held at his resort in the County Clare village of Doonbeg - this weekend as part of a two-day visit to Ireland.

McIlroy has previously played golf with Trump, who earlier this year praised the Northern Irishman's accomplishments on the course after winning back-to-back Masters titles.

"It's going to be different, but the one thing I'd say is his golf resorts have hosted PGA Tour events, European Tour events, LIV events," McIlroy told BBC Sport NI's Stephen Watson.

"He's a big fan of golf, he's a wonderful supporter of golf. He's got a beautiful property here in Doonbeg - it's the first time I've played it. I wouldn't say it's a true links golf course, it's a bit of an Americanised version of a links course, but it's still a great golf course and should provide a good test for the week.

"It's going to be different with him being here but we're here to play a golf tournament and it's a good golf course and keep our head down and play."

During his long-planned visit to Ireland, Trump will meet Irish President Catherine Connolly and hold a bilateral meeting with the Taoiseach [Irish prime minister] Micheal Martin.

He may also present the Irish Open winner with the trophy on Sunday evening amid a significantly enhanced security presence at the property he purchased in 2014.

"I think the weekend, especially when he's here [will feel different], crowds will be limited," added McIlroy.

"Obviously, there's a lot that goes on. So, logistically, it provides some challenges, absolutely. But at the same time, if he wants to come and watch the Irish Open, who are we to say no?"

'We'll see' - Rahm unaffected by LIV 'turbulence'

Trump set to attend star-studded Irish Open at Doonbeg

Six-time major winner McIlroy headlines a strong field at Doonbeg that also features LIV players such as Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Tom McKibbin.

The 2026 LIV season ended early following the cancellation of its team championship in Michigan amid ongoing uncertainty surrounding the tour's future.

On Tuesday, two-time major winner Rahm was tight-lipped about his future and said he was not fretting about the "turbulence" away from the course.

"It's a hard one - I wouldn't want to be in their shoes at the minute and I think just the headspace that it's taken up with the guys, fighting for money or the contracts or where they're going to be playing over the next few years," said McIlroy, 37.

"It's more like the uncertainty for them and it would be nice I think for everyone just to have a bit of certainty around the game and know what's going on and where certain players are going to be playing.

"I'm obviously glad that I'm not really a part of that and I know what I'm going to be doing the next few years, but for everyone involved it would be nice to have certainty and just sort of move forward."

Like Rahm, McIlroy hopes to join European legends Seve Ballesteros, Bernhard Langer, Nick Faldo and Colin Montgomerie on three Irish Open wins after capturing his second title at the K Club last year.

McIlroy also finished runner-up to Rasmus Hojgaard at Royal County Down in 2024 and the world number two believes he is "more relaxed" playing in front of home crowds having also secured a top-10 finish in last year's Open Championship at Royal Portrush.

"I probably went a few years where I wasn't very proud of how I played in the Irish Open," said McIlroy, whose first Irish Open success also came at the K Club in 2016.

"I sort of struggled to deal with the obligations or the pressure or whatever it was, but I think I'm a little bit more relaxed about it these days.

"It's nice to have been able to win it a couple of times and I think coming back after the year that I've had and winning another Masters...I still feel pressure at times playing golf, but coming back to a home crowd and a home open, that shouldn't be one of those."

McIlroy, who finished the PGA Tour play-offs with back-to-back top-four finishes, begins his title defence at 13:35 BST on Thursday. He has been grouped with five-time major winner Brooks Koepka and European Ryder Cup team-mate Robert MacIntyre.

articles.title: Ryan Gerard overtakes Justin Thomas in Official World Golf Ranking
articles.summary: Ryan Gerard moved ahead of Justin Thomas in the latest Official World Golf Ranking update for September 8.
articles.body:

articles.body:
Yin has not completed a 72-hole tournament since May, having missed the cut at the US Women's Open in June before withdrawing mid-tournament from the KPMG Women's PGA Championship later that month due to illness.

The two-time LPGA Tour winner qualified second in the US Solheim Cup points list despite missing the final two majors of the season with the undisclosed stomach issue, which saw her lose around 2.5 stone in weight.

Yin missed the cut by 13 shots on her only LPGA Tour star since at the FM Championship, although Stanford says that the 27-year-old can still play a role in helping Team USA attempt to retain the trophy at Bernardus Golf.

"She's here and she has played two practice rounds," Stanford said in her press conference. "She will play, because that's in the spirit of this competition.

"Every time we play a Solheim Cup, there is a captain's agreement and in that we stipulate who should play how many matches. It's been a while now for the Solheim, that players will play once before Sunday for sure.

"We're still trying to gauge and we're watching, but she's here. She's very happy to be here and she's playing."

Lilia Vu is on-site in the Netherlands for Team USA and was seen in uniform during Tuesday's practice session, with the former world No 1 - who had the clinching half-point in the 2024 victory - a potential last-minute option if required.

The United States are chasing the first victory on European soil since 2015 and their first back-to-back wins in the biennial contest since 2017, with Stanford having faith in her side to enjoy a famous away success.

"When you play in Europe, you have to be mentally tough and you have to be together as a team," Stanford explained. "I think they have it, I really do - they're all on the same page.

"We've talked about it leading up to this event. We're going to talk about it again before we go out and play Thursday night. There's nothing that I need to say to them, because they want to win too.

"The golf itself is so good that you're going to see great golf. It's just what do you have deep down that can get you over the finish line."

Stanford added: "They all seem to be in a good space. We're not peaking yet. They're just getting settled, they're trying to learn the golf course and they're hitting great shots. So it's been fun to watch.

"Peaking would hopefully be leading each session, and I hope it starts Friday morning."

Sky Sports+ will have live coverage of the closing ceremony from 5.30pm on Sunday, following the Solheim Cup winner being crowned, while the opening ceremony on Thursday at 4.30pm will see the opening-day pairings revealed.

articles.title: UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response
articles.summary: Britain's foreign secretary accuses settlers of carrying out the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians, as Israel responds by shutting the UK consulate in East Jerusalem.
articles.body:
The UK has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, accusing Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts".

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded by accusing him of spreading an "outrageous lie" and announced counter-measures including shutting the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem.

The UK sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers

How Israel is expanding settlements in drive to reshape West Bank

The sanctions were launched alongside France and Canada, which in a joint statement with the UK said the action "marks a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution".

Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.

In a statement to MPs, Miliband said: "The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

"And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians."

He said ethnic cleansing was defined by the UN as a "purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent means another ethnic or religious group from certain areas".

Miliband said the official view of the government was that the Israeli occupation of the West Bank was unlawful because of the "entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty, and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements".

He said this position, which is in line with a 2024 advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice, should be reflected in the UK's "economic relationship" with the occupied West Bank.

As a result, over the next six to nine months, the UK will introduce "a new comprehensive sanctions regime", he said.

The foreign secretary also announced a ban on advertising illegal West Bank settlements in the UK.

"The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel," Miliband added.

Later on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the targeted measures were "aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution".

Announcing the closure of the consulate - which represents the UK government in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza - Israel's Foreign Minister Saar said at a press conference: "We know that we have many friends in Britain.

"Unfortunately, we have a hostile Labour government that is consistently operating against the State of Israel, and it has left us no choice but to respond to its hostile actions."

He added that 11 UK MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott and all five sitting Green Party MPs, would be banned from entering Israel, accusing them of "antisemitic and anti-Israel activity".

The UK also issued a joint statement with 11 other countries; France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden.

It said the group was unequivocally committed to the two-state solution and would introduce national measures or support European restrictions on trading goods with West Bank settlements.

The UK announcement comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation. Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.

Miliband told the Commons the UK's "new approach" was necessary because plans for the E1 development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

Elsewhere, he said the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, carried "terrible echoes of the centuries of persecution of the Jewish people" and stressed Israel had "the right to protect its people and defend its territory".

However, he added, "that cannot justify what has happened in Gaza".

He said: "International humanitarian law imposes clear rules for states fighting wars, including to ensure access to food and medical supplies, to avoid mass displacement of civilians, and to avoid the targeting of civilians. Serious and international violations of this law, if proven, amount to war crimes.

"What has occurred, including the actions of the IDF (Israel Defense Forces), have been examined in depth by a number of organisations, including the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry.

"The conclusions of these reports represent increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed, and we support legal processes to determine this."

He added it was up to international courts to determine if Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

Israel's leaders have consistently rejected allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. They have insisted that Israeli forces have operated in accordance with international law.

Miliband began his statement to the Commons by referring to his Jewish roots and childhood experiences of visiting Israel, as well as recent antisemitic attacks in the UK.

He described himself as "a proud British Jew" and outlined his steadfast support for the state of Israel.

He said: "My personal story and that of thousands of British Jews is one of the many reasons why I say to anyone here or around the world who questions Israel's right to exist as a homeland for the Jewish people - you are wrong, and we will call you out whenever you engage in this attempt at the erasure of Israel."

But the UK's Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was a "truly a dark day for British Jews", saying the sanctions were "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric" that would embolden people who "use hatred as a weapon against Jews".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews expressed "deep regret" over Tuesday's announcement, and urged both the UK and Israeli governments to "avoid pursuing what appear to be party interests over national interests".

Responding in the Commons, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat claimed ministers were "enacting policies that the Foreign Office knows won't work".

He agreed that illegal settlements were wrong and "some Israeli ministers have indulged in hateful propaganda and incitement" but added "this isn't about Israel alone and it certainly isn't about reducing the complexity of the region to a single sentence. Sadly, the government is in the process of doing just that".

Israel's foreign minister Saar said on Tuesday evening he had spoken with Tugendhat and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, thanking them "for their firm opposition to the hostile Labour government's announcement today and its series of anti-Israel policies since taking office".

He also said British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel would be removed, and UK activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria - how the Israeli government refers to the West Bank - would be terminated.

Speaking earlier on Tuesday, the country's President Isaac Herzog said the decision would "fall on the wrong side of history", adding: "In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation."

Herzog said the move would directly harm Palestinians and urged foreign governments to turn towards "constructive dialogue" and cooperation, adding "sanctions are not a solution".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the White House had no comment on the joint action, adding that "obviously we're not going to do what the UK did".

Earlier, Donald Trump's ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee earlier told the BBC that the US - Israel's most powerful ally - would "without a doubt" respond to the expected sanctions, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses".

He suggested action could be taken by individual US states as well as at a central, federal level.

The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".

As part of the UK announcement, Miliband also announced sanctions on the financing wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group.

New sanctions in line with the US and European Union were also announced on Iran.

The intervention comes almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.

Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition.

The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Palestinian armed group Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.

Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title: Jon Rahm dodges questions about wanting a pathway back to PGA Tour with LIV Golf future a complete unknown
articles.summary: Jon Rahm says he has "no updates" on LIV Golf's future ahead of the Irish Open, with bankruptcy concerns and funding questions looming large.
articles.body: With complete uncertainty surrounding LIV Golf and whether the circuit will even exist in 2027, the question of where LIV players tee it up next year remains top of mind. That's not just the reality from those on the outside looking in, because Jon Rahm doesn't appear to know where he'll be competing in the new year, either. Rahm, who has won LIV's individual title every season since joining the circuit ahead of the 2024 campaign, is gearing up to play in a few DP World Tour events in the coming weeks. Speaking ahead of this week's Irish Open, he explained he has "no updates" about LIV and its future since the conclusion of the season in August in Indianapolis. LIV Golf lost its funding from the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund (PIF) at the conclusion of the 2026 campaign. LIV CEO Scott O'Neil has announced that a new investor has been secured for "LIV 2.0" to take shape, but reports of a potential bankruptcy filing and funding question marks make the circuit's future uncertain, to put it mildly. LIV GOLF CEO QUIETS SPECULATION WITH ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW INVESTOR TO KEEP CIRCUIT AFLOAT INTO 2027 While Rahm's "no updates" remark was in response to the lone LIV Golf-related question he received during his formal pre-tournament press conference, BBC Sport pressed him multiple times about what his future may hold. "There's just a lot of things in place. There's a lot of things that could happen," Rahm told the outlet. "It's one of those things with time, time's going to tell." When asked if he would like to see a pathway back for him to return to the PGA Tour, the Spaniard didn't exactly offer a straightforward answer. "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I am more than willing to fulfill," Rahm began. "Like I said, time will tell." When asked if he'd like to go back and play on the PGA Tour, he simply stated, "We'll see what happens." LIV GOLF CEO SAYS LEAGUE IS HOPEFUL IT CAN 'DO RIGHT BY' VENDORS SUING THEM OVER ALLEGED MISSED PAYMENTS Rahm is reportedly owed in excess of nine figures on his LIV Golf contract, and, to use his own phrase, time will tell if he will be compensated for his full deal if LIV files for bankruptcy. On top of understandably practicing patience about being paid on his contract, there isn't much else Rahm or any other LIV player can do at this point when it comes to pledging allegiance to a certain side. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Just as it is entirely unclear what LIV 2.0 may or may not look like, it's also a complete unknown as to what a potential pathway back to the PGA Tour could look like for any players who jumped to the breakaway circuit. It is safe to assume some form of a pathway back will be offered to players, especially for a high-profile player such as Rahm, but until something takes shape, the wait-and-see game is the only one to play.

articles.title: LIV Golf: Players free to leave after competition files for bankruptcy protection
articles.summary: LIV Golf intends to starts its new league early next year after filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States.
articles.body:
LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding - a move that means all its players will have the option to leave.

A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business", was filed in the United States on Tuesday.

The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding.

LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future.

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.

Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process.

However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours.

'Time will tell' - Rahm on LIV Golf future

Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0

Saudi Arabia to stop funding LIV Golf next season

Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by PIF, with major winners including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.

However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players to make the new league a reality.

DeChambeau said at the conclusion of that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and he believed there was "something fun coming".

Speaking on Tuesday before this week's Irish Open, Rahm was tight-lipped when pressed on his future.

Asked if he knew what the coming months held, he told BBC Sport: "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis.

"There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell."

Rahm added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell."

The bankruptcy filing was made in the federal district court of New Jersey, where LIV Golf set up a subsidiary earlier in the summer.

Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.

PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.

When announcing its decision to withdraw funding, PIF said the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy.

Despite its decision to stop bankrolling LIV Golf, PIF added it "remains committed" to its "substantial current and future investments in various sports as a priority sector".

On Tuesday, LIV confirmed international investment firm BC Partners as its proposed new investor in a letter to fans outlining its "next phase".

"LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality," said the letter.

"Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf."

O'Neil added in a statement: "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem."

In yet another indication the free-spending days of LIV 1.0 are over, the letter said the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model".

Players are set to be given equity and individual commercial rights are set to be returned to players, giving them greater earning potential. In terms of prize money, LIV Golf purses are set to be lower than events on the PGA Tour - which has risen in part because of the existence of LIV - but higher than events on the DP World Tour.

The letter also outlined proposed changes, with field sizes expanding to 75 players, the introduction of a cut, creating qualifiers and having more teams that "embrace national identities", with the ambitions for teams to "grow into enduring global sports businesses".

articles.title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy in latest step to survive after losing PIF funding, chaotic 2026 season
articles.summary: LIV Golf had been laying the groundwork for bankruptcy for months after losing PIF funding.
articles.body:
LIV Golf officially filed for bankruptcy on Tuesday, a step many had expected to come months after Saudi Arabian funding had been pulled from the league.

LIV Golf announced on Tuesday that it had entered into chapter 11 bankruptcy in the United States. The restructuring, the league said, was done in an effort to allow the league to survive now without Public Investment Fund backing — something that Saudi Arabia announced months ago it would no longer provide after the 2026 campaign.

"The people of LIV Golf, led by the players, have continued to show incredible resilience, commitment, and a shared belief in what we are building. Thanks to their tireless work, LIV Golf has created a foundation to entertain and inspire the next generation of global golf fans around the world," LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil said in a statement. "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf – one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem.

"We are excited about what lies ahead and yet, there is still much to accomplish in the months ahead. We believe deeply in LIV Golf's future, the opportunity in front of us, and the people who will help us realize it."

LIV Golf also said that the PIF has agreed to provide nearly $50 million in debtor-in-possession financing, and that it is seeking similar bankruptcy proceedings in England and Wales.

BC Partners, a London-based private equity firm, will finance the league's attempted return in 2027.

LIV Golf trying to transition into LIV 2.0

The PIF announced back in April that it would no longer fund LIV Golf after it had reportedly invested more than $5 billion into the league since its inception. That has led to plenty of problems for LIV Golf in the months that followed.

The league was hit with multiple lawsuits and had two events canceled, including the team championship in Michigan last month. LIV was reportedly running on loans for months, too, and had been delayed in paying players from its Bedminster tournament in New Jersey.

Multiple notable golfers have already left LIV Golf, and are either back on the PGA Tour already or are preparing to do so. Jon Rahm has been rumored to be considering a departure , and he's listed as the top unsecured creditor in the bankruptcy filing ahead of Bryson DeChambeau. They are still owed millions of dollars. DeChambeau's contract with LIV Golf expired at the end of the season.

While specifics aren't yet known, the restructuring could result in LIV Golf members being released from their existing contracts.

O'Neil and LIV Golf announced that it had secured an investor to keep the league afloat in 2027, though details surrounding that agreement — including who the investor actually is — are very scarce. And the league will certainly need more money.

All of that, and the fact that LIV Golf had been reportedly laying the groundwork for bankruptcy in the United States for months, make Tuesday's announcement very unsurprising.

The move to "LIV 2.0" is expected to take months to finalize. The league announced mass layoffs last month , too, a restructuring that many had seen coming for months. LIV Golf is hoping to put out a 10-event schedule in 2027, five events in the United States and five tournaments internationally.

But that's still a long way off, and plenty has to be figured out before that can happen. Filing for bankruptcy is a notable step, but it is far from the last one the league will have to make in the coming months.

"Now it is time to enter the next phase of LIV Golf," O'Neil wrote in a letter to fans. "Today, we took an important step forward to get there. articles.title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy as it attempts to restart in 2027
articles.summary: LIV Golf, the Saudi-funded tour that once aimed to take over professional golf, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Tuesday as it attempts to restructure and restart what it called its “next chapter.”
articles.body: LIV Golf, the Saudi-funded tour that once aimed to take over professional golf, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Tuesday as it attempts to restructure and restart what it called its “next chapter.” LIV Golf Chief Executive Scott O’Neil said in a statement that he believed deeply in the future of the tour, which plans to “begin its new era in early 2027.” “This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf — one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem,” O’Neil said. “We are excited about what lies ahead and yet, there is still much to accomplish in the months ahead.” The bankruptcy filing in U.S. bankruptcy court in New Jersey comes five years after the tour launched with enormous fanfare and the financial backing of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, with ambitions no less than supplanting the PGA Tour as golf's pre-eminent tour. LIV initially signed some of the sport’s biggest names, but its format — which included 54-hole tournaments and team competitions with names like "Crushers GC" — never caught on, and a proposed 2023 merger with the PGA Tour never became final. Speculation about LIV Golf's future began in mid-April, fueled by unconfirmed reports of an “emergency summit” in New York City featuring LIV Golf’s top executives on the eve of a tour stop in Mexico City. The PIF — which had sunk a reported $5 billion into LIV — later announced it was rethinking its investment strategy, transitioning "from a period of rapid growth and acceleration to a new phase of sustained value creation." With the PIF’s funding pulled, the league entered a summer of uncertainty, and eventually canceled its season-ending championship in August in Michigan. That same month, O'Neil said the tour had an agreement in place with a new lead investor, but did not disclose who it was. As part of its bankruptcy filing Tuesday, LIV announced in a statement that it is aiming to restart with the help of BC Partners. To help keep LIV running as it navigates the bankruptcy process, LIV said it received debtor-in-possession loan of $49.6 million from the Saudi Arabia PIF. LIV’s filing listed its golfers as its largest creditors, with Jon Rahm ($7.47 million), Bryson DeChambeau ($5.76 million) Dustin Johnson ($5.48 million) and Cameron Smith ($4.85 million) listed as having the largest claims. The company estimated its assets are worth between $100 million and $500 million, and its liabilities between $500 million to $1 billion. Almost immediately after its launching in 2021, LIV Golf drew criticism as “sportswashing,” an example of Saudi Arabia using high-profile investments into sports as a way to distract from the country’s human rights record, soften its image globally and build influence within the U.S. “If sportswashing is going to increase my GDP by 1%, then we will continue doing sportswashing,” Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told Fox News in 2023. Just as quickly, LIV drew the ire of the PGA Tour, the organizer of a majority of pro golf events, by signing many of the sport’s best-known players and past major champions such as Brooks Koepka, Bryson DeChambeau, Phil Mickelson and Dustin Johnson to lucrative contracts to play on its breakaway tour. When the PGA Tour suspended players who had resigned their PGA membership to take part in LIV competitions, then LIV-CEO Greg Norman, the former star golfer, wrote a letter to the PGA Tour's commissioner complaining that it was a move to "intimidate players by bullying and threatening them." In 2023, the PGA Tour and LIV Golf announced a surprise merger to end their court battles. The decision sparked investigations by U.S. senators and the Justice Department. In a hearing concerning the partnership of the former golf rivals, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said the hearing was “about how a brutal, repressive regime can buy influence, indeed even take over a cherished American institution to cleanse its public image.” Entering its fifth season this year, LIV’s big ambitions and roster of big-name players took a hit, however, when Koepka and a second major champion, Patrick Reed, left the tour in January. (In the bankruptcy filing, Koepka is listed as a creditor, with a claim of $1.7 million.) Soon after, Koepka played in a PGA Tour event. The defections followed the PGA’s decision to offer a small number of players who had left for LIV a pathway to return to playing in PGA events. Though LIV plans to re-emerge next year, it will need players to sign on and Rahm, a former Masters champion who is one of its biggest former names, was noncommittal this week when asked about his future. “There’s a lot of things that could happen, and it’s one of those things where time’s gonna tell,” Rahm told the BBC.

articles.title: LIV Golf files for US bankruptcy protection but reveals 2027 plans as players face uncertain future
articles.summary: LIV Golf released a statement on Tuesday regarding the league's future; Sky News understands LIV Golf are entering talks with players about whether they take part in the new iteration or elect to leave
articles.body:
On Tuesday the golf league announced it had entered into bankruptcy protection in an attempt to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its financial backing.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced earlier this year they would not bankroll the league beyond the 2026 campaign, having spent over $5bn (£3.6bn) over five years, leaving the circuit searching for fresh investment in recent months.

LIV Golf cut around 90 per cent of their staff after the conclusion of the season, as talks continued over their long-term future, with BC Partners later named as the proposed new investors.

A statement from the league on Tuesday confirmed they had entered bankruptcy protection, while Sky News understands LIV Golf are entering talks with players about whether they take part in the new iteration or elect to leave.

LIV Golf say a Chapter 11 petition has been filed to "preserve the company's business as a going concern through an innovative player-first ownership model".

In a statement on Tuesday, LIV Golf said the league is expected to be majority-owned by its players, with whom it "remains in advanced discussions".

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said: "The people of LIV Golf, led by the players, have continued to show incredible resilience, commitment, and a shared belief in what we are building. Thanks to their tireless work, LIV Golf has created a foundation to entertain and inspire the next generation of global golf fans around the world.

"This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem. We are excited about what lies ahead and yet, there is still much to accomplish in the months ahead.

"We believe deeply in LIV Golf's future, the opportunity in front of us, and the people who will help us realise it. We are grateful to our players, the incredible team at LIV Golf, our board, BC Partners, and our partners all over the world standing tall with us, and we thank them for their belief in our next chapter. A special thank you to Ducera Partners who drove this investment process. We will not rest until we deliver on LIV Golf's full potential."

What are LIV Golf's plans for next season?

LIV Golf remain hopeful of launching a new iteration of the league in 2027, with events planned in "places like" Australia, South Africa, Mexico, England, Hong Kong and the United States.

Their proposal includes expanding fields to 75 players, with cuts and additional pathways - including Monday qualifiers - added to their events, with more teams embracing national identities.

"I have often said that our role in golf should be to complete, not compete," O'Neil added. "I believe that more strongly today than ever. I know that the next phase of LIV Golf will be an important part of a healthier global golf ecosystem.

"It will create more opportunity for players, bring elite golf to more parts of the world, and give teams and players a real stake in the future they are building.

"Transitions are rarely easy, but they are powerful when you know where you are going. And we do."

LIV Golf's announcement came just hours after Jon Rahm told reporters he still had a contract that he was "more than willing to fulfil", with the Spaniard still reportedly having more than $100m remaining on the multi-year contract signed at the end of 2023.

Rahm was one of three players to reject the PGA Tour's Returning Player Program introduced earlier this year, with Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith also electing against taking the same pathway back that Brooks Koepka accepted.

All three past major champions are among LIV Golf's largest creditors, with Dustin Johnson understood to be another, while PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp said at the Tour Championship there was no plan to reintroduce the program for next season.

There is still plenty to be determined, but It could leave them all facing a similar journey back to the PGA Tour that Patrick Reed currently faces. The Masters champion is set for a card via finishing inside the top 10 of the DP World Tour's Race to Dubai rankings.

Many of LIV Golf participants were still active DP World Tour members and could elect to play their next season, although it remains unclear whether players would be able to compete on both circuits - like has been seen in recent years - going forward.

articles.title: LIV Golf Files for Bankruptcy as Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm, More Free to Leave Organization
articles.summary: LIV Golf reportedly could lose some of its biggest stars after filing for bankruptcy.
articles.body:
LIV Golf reportedly could lose some of its biggest stars after filing for bankruptcy.

Doug Ferguson of the Associated Press reported Tuesday the breakaway golf league, which was initially funded by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund that has since pulled its financial backing, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection with more than $500 million in debt.

According to Ferguson, such a decision "was widely expected" and done so as "part of its goal to revive the league without Saudi funding." LIV also said it agreed to a restructuring plan with BC Partners serving as the primary source of capital.

Laura Scott of BBC reported LIV owes at least $45 million to players such as Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, who "now have the option to leave."

While Scott noted it remains to be seen when players who left could discuss joining other golf tours, even those who signed multi-year contracts with LIV are no longer obligated to stay on for the LIV 2.0 version the league hopes to launch.

Part of the bankruptcy filing included documents that show how much money is owed to LIV Golf's creditors. That list includes Rahm ($7.5 million), DeChambeau ($5.7 million), Dustin Johnson ($5.5 million), Cameron Smith ($4.8 million), Tyrell Hatton ($3.4 million) and Brooks Koepka ($1.7 million).

Koepka previously left LIV to return to the PGA Tour but was at one point one of the breakaway league's biggest stars.

Golf.com noted the Saudi PIF will still provide $49.6 million in financing under a debtor-in-possession agreement.

As Ferguson detailed, LIV CEO Scott O'Neil has detailed plans for a LIV 2.0 that would feature a reduced schedule, expanded fields and a 54-hole cut. What's more, players would have equity in the league.

Tuesday's filing comes after LIV already canceled the final event of its 2026 season, which was scheduled to take place in Michigan.

While Koepka and Patrick Reed already left and the future of the league is tenuous at best, losing golfers such as Rahm or DeChambeau would be quite the blow to the overall outlook of its future plans.

articles.title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy in latest fallout for breakaway tour
articles.summary: LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Tuesday with more than $500 million in debt, part of its goal to revive the league without Saudi funding.
articles.body: LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Tuesday in New Jersey with more than $500 million in debt, part of its goal to revive the league without Saudi funding. The move was widely expected after the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia abruptly ended its financial support this year. The final event was last month in Indiana. Four vendors already have filed lawsuits because they have not been paid. LIV said it has agreed to a restructuring plan with BC Partners as the primary source of its capital. “This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf,” CEO Scott O’Neil said in a news release. O’Neil has said “LIV Golf 2.0” would feature players as majority owners in a reduced schedule. In a letter to LIV Golf fans, O’Neil said the new look would expand the size of the field from 57 to 75 players and introduce a 54-hole cut for the first time. There also would be Monday qualifiers. He said the team concept would be built around nationalities and that LIV would continue to tap some of its more successful markets in Australia, South Africa and Asia. Still, the new version would be a shell of what LIV promised when it launched in June 2022 after paying nine-figure signing bonuses to lure away top names from the PGA Tour. The excessive spending topped more than $5 billion before PIF said in April it was pulling the plug. Still to be determined is the future of the biggest stars still with LIV, most notably Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau. Rahm is playing the Irish Open this week and told BBC Northern Ireland: “I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I’m more than willing to fulfill. Like I said, time will tell.” Rahm, DeChambeau, Dustin Johnson and Cameron Smith were the leading four creditors listed in the filing. Of the top 30 creditors LIV listed, 14 were players. The filing listed only the “unsecured claim” — Rahm led the list at nearly $7.5 million — and not the full amount owed. LIV listed between $100 million and $500 million in estimated assets, and $500 million and $1 billion in liabilities. The state of Louisiana is listed among the largest creditors at $1,220,000. LIV Golf postponed its event in Louisiana shortly after PIF announced it was ending its support. The Michigan event also was canceled, with the team championship merged into the final event in Indiana. Chapter 11 is commonly known as reorganization bankruptcy and generally allows the debtor to continue to operate the business, even borrowing new money under court approval. LIV Golf said the PIF has agreed to provide $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing through the DIP credit agreement, subject to the court’s approval. BC Partners L.P. — the credit business of UK-based BC Partners — and other minority investors that might emerge would provide the exit financing as LIV tries to keep going. LIV said it intends to emerge from bankruptcy and start its new version as early as 2027. “Now it is time to enter the next phase of LIV Golf,” O’Neil said in his letter. “Today, we took an important step forward to get there. LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the League’s next phase a reality. “Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf.” But so much depends on who stays. The PGA Tour has banned players for one year from their most recent LIV Golf appearance. Brooks Koepka was the first LIV player to return under penalty — a $5 million payment to charity, no equity grants for five years, no access to bonus money the year he returned. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp offered the same deal to Rahm, DeChambeau and Smith with a tight deadline to accept. None did, and three months later as the U.S.-Iran war took root, PIF pulled its funding and sent LIV Golf into a spiral. Rolapp has not been inclined to discuss any paths back while players are under contract. O’Neil said LIV Golf’s intention was to “complete, not compete,” a phrase that rankled more stable tours because of the disruption LIV Golf created under former CEO Greg Norman who felt players should be able to compete on any tour, while be required to play a full schedule on LIV.

articles.title: Packers sign RB Damon Bankston
articles.summary: Damon Bankston was brought in as a pre-draft visitor this spring and had a tryout in Green Bay on Tuesday
articles.body:
Sports Illustrated 's Bill Huber is reporting that the Green Bay Packers have signed rookie running back Damon Bankston , filling their final vacancy on the team's practice squad. Bankston was brought into Green Bay initially as a pre-draft visitor , but he ended up signing with the New York Giants as an undrafted free agent for $115,000 guaranteed, while the Packers opted to add Jaden Nixon — who was not kept on the practice squad after cuts — for $15,000 guaranteed.

The New Mexico product is an interesting prospect, as he posted a 4.43-second 40-yard dash during the pre-draft process but was overlooked by the major all-star games because he was a member of a committee backfield. At the college level, Bankston contributed not only as a one-cut runner, but also as a pass-catcher and a returner. Before transferring up to the FBS level, he was an all-conference player at Weber State in the FCS.

It appears that the Packers are transitioning to an outside zone-based offense, similar to what head coach Matt LaFleur ran earlier in his tenure in Green Bay . For what it's worth, Bankston is a very good fit for that scheme.

Bankston had a workout with the Packers on Tuesday, and the following players were also brought in:

It's possible that Green Bay is still looking for answers to practice squad bodies at quarterback, where they signed Kedon Slovis from the Arizona Cardinals , and tight end, where the team retained Drake Dabney, but it also makes a lot of sense that they're keeping an eye on defensive backs, too. The team only has 11 total defensive backs available between the 53-man roster and the practice squad, barely enough to make a two-deep at the position once you include nickel defenders. Eventually, the Packers will probably want to add numbers somewhere on the team in the secondary.

articles.title: Jon Rahm willing to fulfill contract with 'LIV 1.0,' he says in interview
articles.summary: Jon Rahm is playing the Irish Open this week amid questions about his future.
articles.body:
Jon Rahm is playing the Irish Open this week amid questions about his future, and not just a busy schedule of as many as five DP World Tour events, depending on the birth of his fourth child.

The big question is his future with LIV Golf, which has lost the financial backing of Saudi Arabia.

"There's just a lot of things in place. There's a lot of things that could happen. It's one of those things with time, time's going to tell," Rahm said Tuesday to BBC Northern Ireland.

Most telling was when he was asked if he would like to see a path back to the PGA Tour, similar to what was offered to Brooks Koepka. There's also the route of Patrick Reed, who played a full European tour schedule this year and will earn one of 10 PGA Tour cards.

"I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfill," Rahm said. "Like I said, time will tell."

Pressed again on whether he'd like to play the PGA Tour, Rahm smiled and shrugged when he said, "We'll see what happens."

LIV Golf announced Tuesday that it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection as part of a restructuring agreement with BC Partners.
